title: The peace that doesn't end
hookLine: Nachiketa turned down Death's gifts because they wouldn't last; chapter five names the peace that does
carry: lasting peace comes from the friend of all beings
tomorrow: Lift the self by the self
last: THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BODY.

cards: Remember Nachiketa, the boy at Death's door from day two? Death offered him gold, horses, a long life, music, anything, if only he'd drop his question. And the boy said: keep them.
They won't last past tomorrow. Now think of the best meal of last month. Where is it now?
Wonderful, and over by the end of the plate. The new phone, the great weekend, the compliment that made your whole Tuesday. Each one arrived, glowed, and left.
The last verses of Gita chapter five ask Nachiketa's question: where's the happiness that doesn't end?

teach.b: Verse twenty-two: the pleasures born of contact, of the senses touching their objects, are wombs of sorrow. They have a beginning and an end, and the wise don't take their delight in them.

A womb is where something grows: every pleasure that depends on something outside carries, inside it, the sorrow of its ending. Nobody here says pleasure is evil. Verse twenty-three sets a practical test.

teach.h: BEAR THE PUSH OF DESIRE AND ANGER.
teach.b: Whoever can bear the rush of desire and anger here, in this life, is a yogi, a happy person. Not someone who never feels desire or anger. Someone who can bear the push of it.
Verse twenty-four gives the other direction: happy within, delighting within, lit from within. That person reaches brahma-nirvana, the stillness of Brahman. Yes, nirvana: the word is in the Gita too.
And the chapter's last verse names the source.
The one who knows Krishna as the one who receives every offering, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, reaches peace. Shanti.
That's a core Hindu teaching: lasting joy isn't something you collect; it's found within, in God, the friend of all beings.
It's why so many Hindu prayers end om shanti, shanti, shanti. And it meets you in the quiet after something good ends, the trip, the show, the party. That ache isn't failure.
It's the Gita pointing you where to look next.

how: Hindu prayers and readings often close with 'om shanti shanti shanti', a threefold wish for peace, and some practitioners use steady, even breathing like that of Gita 5.27–28 to settle before meditation.

o: a peace that doesn't come and go
a pleasure that lasts a while

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.

s: the word nirvana appears in the Bhagavad Gita
verse 24 speaks of brahma-nirvana, the stillness of Brahman.
verse 23 says a yogi never feels desire or anger
the yogi is the one who can bear the push of desire and anger, in this life.
the Gita says pleasures are evil
it says they have a beginning and an end, so the wise don't rest their delight in them.

games.q: desire and anger come pushing in. what does verse 23 say makes someone a yogi?
o: bearing their push, here in this life.
acting on them quickly to get rid of them.
games.why: bearing the push, here, before leaving the body. the Gita's test isn't feeling nothing; it's not being swept away.

practice: Sit tall and even out the breath, the way verses twenty-seven and twenty-eight describe, the air moving quietly in and out through the nostrils. If a want or an irritation pushes in, bear it for one breath and let it pass.
Then, softly, out loud or under your breath, say what so many Hindu prayers end with: om shanti, shanti, shanti. If you don't pray, just say peace, three times, and listen to the quiet after.

wordCard.voice: Shanti. Peace: not the pleasure that begins and ends, but the peace of the one who knows the friend of all beings.

orig.note: Sanskrit: shanti, peace; the last word of chapter five's promise (5.29).

carryVoice: Carry this: lasting peace comes from the friend of all beings. The kind that doesn't end when the plate does. Chapter five, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.29 (friend of all beings; peace)
Katha Upanishad 1.1.23–1.1.29 (Nachiketa refuses Death's gifts as lasting only till tomorrow)
